subject: math

unit.title: Fractions of shapes and quantities
unit.essentialQuestion: What does each part of a fraction tell us, and how do we find a fraction of a number?

title: Thirds and quarters of shapes
objectives: By the end, I can find ⅓, ¼ and ¾ of a shape and explain that the parts must be equal.

vocabulary.definition: parts that are exactly the same size — they land on top of each other when folded
vocabulary.example: a strip folded into 3 matching pieces
fold a strip in three — each part is ⅓
one slice of a bar cut into 4 equal slices

vocabulary.definition: three of the four equal parts
vocabulary.example: shade 3 of 4 equal parts — that's ¾

vocabulary.definition: the bottom number — it says how many equal parts the whole is cut into
vocabulary.example: the 3 in ⅓ means three equal parts

emphasize: The parts must be EQUAL — a fraction is only real if the pieces match exactly.
The big reveal: the MORE equal parts you cut, the SMALLER each part is — so ⅓ is smaller than ½, not bigger.
Pre-empt the classic misconception '⅓ > ½ because 3 > 2' — fold the same strip both ways and compare the pieces.

keyConcepts: fractions as equal parts of a whole
the denominator counts the equal parts
misconceptions: '⅓ is bigger than ½ because 3 is bigger than 2'
any split counts — calling three UNEQUAL pieces 'thirds'
hooks: Three friends, one chocolate bar — how do we split it so nobody grumbles?
priorKnowledge: halves and quarters from Year 1 — a fraction is one of EQUAL parts

human: several paper strips and paper circles
a real chocolate bar (or a paper one marked in squares)
the strips within the child's reach for the whole lesson — the AI will ask for folding again during practice
digital: animated fraction bars on the whiteboard block
shading and sorting practice blocks (rendered by the app)

delivery.humanNotes: You run the first ~8 minutes with the REAL chocolate bar and paper strips (hook + concrete explain). The folding is the heart of this lesson — thirds folded like a letter into an envelope, quarters by folding in half twice — and paper in the hands beats any animation. Say the script lines warmly in your own words; the maths and the anchor phrases ('equal parts', 'more pieces means smaller pieces') must stay exact. When you lay the third-strip beside the quarter-strip and say the handoff line, the AI character takes over on screen. Keep the strips and pencils within reach — the AI will ask the child to fold and shade again during the checks and practice.

video.title: Fractions Are a Piece of Cake - Full Episode | Series 8 E24 | Numberblocks
video.watchTask: Every time the Numberblocks split something at the party, shout out whether the parts are EQUAL or NOT equal — only equal parts make real fractions!

afterCheck.question: What had to be true about the pieces before the Numberblocks could share them fairly?
afterCheck.expectedAnswer: The parts had to be equal — all exactly the same size

plan.goal: Set the fairness problem — three friends, one bar; retrieve 'equal' from Year 1 halves.
plan.note: Mime an unfair break (one giant piece, two tiny) and let the child protest — the outrage IS the hook. Don't teach yet.
plan.successCriteria: Child protests the unfair split and says a real half means 'both parts the same / equal'.

script.say: Three friends, one chocolate bar — and everyone wants a fair share. How do we split it so nobody grumbles? What if I break it like THIS — one giant piece for me, two crumbs for you two? … Not fair?! Alright, alright. Quick first: what does 'equal' mean? Last year we made halves and quarters — what made a piece a REAL half?
script.adaptHints: Play the unfair break for laughs and let the child correct you. Listen for 'both parts the same / equal'. If 'equal' is shaky: fold a strip into two matching halves — 'equal means they land exactly on top.'

humanHandoff.setup: Chocolate bar held up; paper strips, circles, pencils and scissors laid out but untouched.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: Not yet — the human continues into the explain beat.

stuckProtocol: If 'equal' is shaky: fold one strip in half and open it — 'two parts that land exactly on top of each other. THAT'S equal.'

plan.goal: Model folding real strips: thirds (letter-fold), quarters (half then half again), shade ¾; reveal that more pieces means smaller pieces.
plan.note: This is the CPA concrete stage and the reason this lesson has a human intro — the child must SEE and FEEL real paper folding. Lay the third-strip beside the quarter-strip for the size reveal before handing off.
plan.successCriteria: Child watches thirds and quarters folded, sees ¾ shaded, and hears 'more pieces means each piece is smaller' with the two strips side by side.

script.say: Watch. To make THIRDS I fold this strip into three equal parts — like a letter going into an envelope. One, two, three — three equal parts. Each one is a third, and we write it ⅓. The bottom number, 3, tells me how many equal parts I made. Now a new strip, folded into FOUR equal parts — half… and half again — quarters, ¼. If I colour three of the four — look — that's three-quarters, ¾. Now the magic bit: I'll put the third-strip right next to the quarter-strip. Look closely — which piece is bigger? The THIRD! More pieces means each piece is smaller. — Right, now my friend on the screen is going to draw some fraction bars for us. Watch!
script.adaptHints: The final sentence is the handoff line — say it as written. Let the child run a finger along both strips to compare the piece sizes.

humanHandoff.setup: A thirds-strip and a quarters-strip (3 of 4 parts shaded) lying side by side in front of the child. Leave them visible — the AI refers back to them.
humanHandoff.cueToResume: When the human says 'Watch!', the AI character starts the next beat.

plan.goal: Move to pictorial: the character draws fraction bars matching the folded strips; the child directs the shading of ⅓ and then names ¾.
plan.note: Bridge concrete → pictorial: the bars on screen mirror the real strips on the table. The child is the boss of the shading.
plan.successCriteria: Child tells the character to shade 1 of 3 parts for ⅓ and correctly names 3 shaded quarters as ¾.

script.say: I saw what you two folded! Let me draw those strips my way. Here's a bar cut into three EQUAL parts — just like your letter-fold. You be the boss: to show one third, how many parts do I colour? … One — and there it is, ⅓! Now my four-part bar. I'm colouring one, two, three of the four equal parts… What fraction have I shaded? … And here's my puzzle back to you: the bottom number of ⅓ is 3 — what is that 3 actually telling us?
script.adaptHints: Pause for the child's answer after each question. If they say 'three quarters' with values, celebrate; if they say '3 out of 4', bridge it: 'yes — three of the four equal parts, three-quarters, ¾.'

check.question: I shaded 3 of 4 equal parts — what fraction is shaded?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the shaded parts (3) and made it the bottom number
wrongAnswers.remedy: The bottom number counts ALL the equal parts. How many parts does the whole bar have?

wrongAnswers.why: muddling shaded with unshaded
wrongAnswers.remedy: Point to the coloured parts and count just those: one, two, three… of how many?

plan.goal: The key diagnostic: which is bigger, ½ or ¼? — catching 'bigger bottom number = bigger piece'.
plan.note: This is the lesson's heart. After the on-screen answer, send the child to the REAL strips to prove it — fold and compare.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers ½ and proves it with the strips (the half-piece is longer).

script.say: Big question — think carefully, it's sneaky. Which is BIGGER: one half, or one quarter? … Now don't just tell me — PROVE it! Grab two strips from your table: fold one into halves, one into quarters, and lay one piece against one piece. What do the strips say?
script.adaptHints: If the child answers ¼ 'because 4 is bigger', don't correct — send them straight to the folding proof and let the paper do the arguing.

blocks.prompt: Which is bigger — ½ or ¼?
options: ½ — fewer pieces means bigger pieces
blocks.explain: Fold the SAME strip into 2 and into 4: the half-piece is twice as long. More cuts make smaller pieces — the bottom number counts pieces, it doesn't measure size!

check.question: Which is bigger — ½ or ¼? Prove it with the strips.
check.expectedAnswer: ½ — folding the same strip into 2 gives longer pieces than folding it into 4

wrongAnswers.why: treating the bigger bottom number as the bigger piece
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fold the SAME strip into 2, then another into 4, and lay one piece on one piece. More cuts, smaller pieces — what do you see?

wrongAnswers.answer: calls an unequal split 'thirds' during the proof
wrongAnswers.why: counting pieces, not EQUAL pieces
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fold the three parts on top of each other. Do they land exactly? If not, they aren't thirds.

plan.goal: Independent folding, shading and sorting: real thirds/quarters vs impostors, ¾ two ways, size comparisons.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. The child may use the real strips for any item — encourage folding on a miss (CPA step down). The equal-parts test ('do they land on top of each other?') is the self-check habit.
plan.successCriteria: Child completes 3+ items correctly including one 'impostor' (unequal split) spotted and one size comparison.

script.say: Practice time, fraction inspector! Some of these shapes are cut into REAL thirds and quarters… and some are impostors — unequal cheats! Your badge question for every one: are the parts EQUAL? Fold your strips any time you want to prove an answer.
script.adaptHints: Frame shaded parts with the child's interests (flag designs, pizza toppings, chocolate flavours). Never change the fractions.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'I think the pieces got counted without checking they're equal' or 'the bigger bottom number tricked us.'
Drop to concrete: fold a real strip and overlay the pieces.
One hint: 'Do the parts land exactly on top of each other?'
Re-ask with halves vs quarters only, then build back to thirds.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — let's take a smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states both rules — equal parts, and more parts means smaller parts; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led recall; the character listens. The chocolate bar can now be shared for real!
plan.successCriteria: Child explains what makes a piece a third (one of THREE EQUAL parts) and why a third beats a quarter.

script.say: In your own words, inspector: what makes a piece a real THIRD? … And which is bigger, a third or a quarter — why? … Exactly! Three EQUAL parts, and fewer pieces means bigger pieces. You checked the parts were equal before you named a single fraction — that's a real mathematician's habit. I think three friends can share that chocolate bar fairly now…
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed: folding to prove, overlaying pieces, spotting impostors. If the real bar is present, let the fair share happen!

block.prompt: A strip is folded into 2 EQUAL parts. What is each part called?
block.explain: Two equal parts — each one is a half, ½. The bottom number 2 counts the equal parts.

wrongAnswers.why: fraction names not yet tied to the number of parts
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the equal parts: two. Which fraction has a 2 on the bottom?

wrongAnswers.why: guessing among the new words
wrongAnswers.remedy: The bottom number counts the parts. Two parts — so the bottom number is…?

hints: Count the equal parts first.
The bottom number = how many equal parts.

reteach.say: The name is hiding in the count! Fold into TWO equal parts → halves. THREE → thirds. FOUR → quarters. Count the parts, and the fraction names itself.

block.caption: The bottom number counts the parts

block.statement: To make real quarters, the 4 parts must all be EQUAL.
block.explain: Yes! Four parts only make quarters if they're exactly the same size — fold them on top of each other to check.

wrongAnswers.why: the lesson's core misconception — any 4 pieces count
wrongAnswers.remedy: Imagine your friend gets a crumb and you get half the bar — are those fair quarters? What went wrong?

hints: Would an unfair split make anyone grumble?
The fold test: do the parts land exactly on top of each other?

reteach.say: Fractions are the fairness police! Four pieces are only QUARTERS if every piece matches exactly. One giant piece and three crumbs is four pieces — but nobody would call that fair, and maths doesn't either.

block.caption: Equal parts = real quarters. Unequal = impostor!

block.prompt: A pizza is cut into 3 EQUAL slices. What is one slice?
options: ⅓ — one of three equal parts
block.explain: Three equal parts — each slice is one third, ⅓. The 3 on the bottom counts the equal slices.

wrongAnswers.why: thirds and quarters muddled
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count the slices: one, two, three. Which fraction has that number on the bottom?

wrongAnswers.why: counted the slices instead of naming the fraction of ONE slice
wrongAnswers.remedy: Three slices altogether, yes — but ONE slice is one out of…? That's the fraction.

hints: Count the equal slices.
One slice out of three equal slices is…?

reteach.say: One pizza, three equal slices. Each slice is one of the three — one third, written ⅓. Bottom number 3: how many equal parts. Top number 1: how many of them you're holding.

block.statement: A bar is cut into 3 pieces: one BIG piece and two tiny ones. Each piece is a third.
block.explain: No — thirds must be three EQUAL pieces. Three unequal pieces are just… three pieces. The fold test would catch it: they don't land on top of each other.

wrongAnswers.why: counting pieces, not equal pieces — the impostor trap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fold the three pieces on top of each other. Do they match exactly? If not, they aren't thirds.

hints: Count is right — but what else must be true?
Would the friend with the tiny piece call that fair?

reteach.say: Three pieces is only HALF the rule. The other half: they must be EQUAL. One big and two tiny pieces fail the fold test — they don't land on top of each other — so no thirds badge for them. Impostors!

block.text: Shade 3 of the 4 equal parts — that's ___-quarters of the shape.

wrongAnswers.why: counted all the parts instead of the shaded ones
wrongAnswers.remedy: The bottom counts ALL parts; the top counts the SHADED ones. How many did you colour?

wrongAnswers.why: defaulted to the unit fraction
wrongAnswers.remedy: One quarter is just ONE part coloured. You coloured more — count them.

hints: Count only the coloured parts.
Top number = coloured parts; bottom = all parts.

reteach.say: ¾ is a team of quarters! One quarter, two quarters, three quarters — three of the four equal parts coloured in. Three on top (what you shaded), four on the bottom (all the parts).

block.prompt: Which is bigger — ½ or ¼?
block.explain: Fold the same strip into 2 and into 4 — the half is twice as long as the quarter. More cuts make smaller pieces.

wrongAnswers.why: bigger bottom number read as bigger piece — the classic trap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fold the SAME strip into 2, then into 4. Lay one piece on one piece — which is longer?

wrongAnswers.why: comparing counts of pieces, not sizes
wrongAnswers.remedy: Same whole strip, different number of cuts — can the pieces be the same size?

hints: Same strip, more cuts — what happens to each piece?
Prove it with your real strips!

reteach.say: Think of sharing one cake: between 2 people or between 4 people — when do you get MORE cake? With fewer sharers! The bottom number counts the sharers, so a BIGGER bottom number means a SMALLER piece. ½ beats ¼.

block.caption: Halves are big, quarters are small — same whole!

block.prompt: Trickier! Which is bigger — ⅓ or ¼?
options: ⅓ — three sharers get more than four
block.explain: Cut the same bar into 3 or into 4: three pieces are each bigger than four pieces. ⅓ > ¼.

wrongAnswers.why: bigger denominator still read as bigger piece
wrongAnswers.remedy: Fold two same-size strips — one into 3, one into 4. Compare one piece with one piece.

wrongAnswers.why: both are 'one piece' so they seem equal
wrongAnswers.remedy: One piece of THREE and one piece of FOUR from the same bar — same size? Fold and check!

hints: Fewer sharers means bigger shares.
Same bar: 3 pieces each bigger, or 4 pieces each bigger?

reteach.say: Line up the fraction pieces from your folded strips like a staircase: the half is the giant, the third is next, the quarter is smallest. Every extra cut shrinks the pieces. So ⅓ beats ¼ — even though 4 looks bigger!

items.text: square cut into 4 matching small squares
strip cut into 4 pieces, all different sizes
bar 'in thirds': one huge piece, two crumbs
pizza in 3 slices — one is half the pizza

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: matching squares, matching wedges, letter-fold → real; different sizes, huge+crumbs, half-pizza slice → impostor

wrongAnswers.answer: any split with the right COUNT goes to 'real'
wrongAnswers.why: counting pieces, ignoring equality
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count is only rule one. Rule two: would the pieces land exactly on top of each other?

hints: Ask both questions: how many parts, AND are they equal?
Imagine folding the parts on top of each other.

reteach.say: An inspector checks TWO things: the count and the match. Four matching wedges? Real quarters. Four random chunks? Impostor — right count, wrong sizes. Equal parts or it isn't a fraction at all.

block.title: The inspector's checklist
steps: Count the parts — does it match the bottom number?
Fold test — would every part land exactly on the others?
Both yes → real fraction. Any no → impostor!

block.prompt: A friend says: '⅓ is bigger than ½, because 3 is bigger than 2.' What would you tell them? How could you PROVE it with paper?
block.sample: The bottom number counts the pieces, it doesn't measure them. Fold the same strip into 2 and into 3 — the half-piece is longer. More pieces means smaller pieces, so ½ > ⅓.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: They're wrong — fold the same strip into 2 and into 3 and compare: the half is bigger, because more parts means smaller parts

wrongAnswers.why: shares the bigger-bottom-number misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Don't argue — fold! Same strip, into 2 and into 3. Lay one piece on one piece. What does the paper say?

hints: What does the bottom number actually count?
The proof is a fold: same strip, 2 parts vs 3 parts.

reteach.say: The bottom number is the number of SHARERS, not the size of the share. Three sharers each get less than two sharers — every time. Fold the same strip both ways and the paper proves it: the half-piece wins.

block.caption: Same strip: halves are bigger than thirds

block.prompt: A flag has 4 equal stripes. 3 are red, 1 is white. What fraction is NOT red?
block.explain: 3 of the 4 stripes are red (¾), so just 1 of the 4 — one quarter, ¼ — is not red. ¾ and ¼ make the whole flag.

wrongAnswers.why: gave the shaded part instead of the unshaded — the '¾ left' muddle
wrongAnswers.remedy: ¾ is the RED part. The question asks about the stripe that ISN'T red — how many of the 4 is that?

wrongAnswers.why: counted 1 white out of 3 red instead of out of ALL parts
wrongAnswers.remedy: The bottom number counts ALL the equal stripes, red and white together. How many stripes altogether?

hints: How many stripes altogether? How many are white?
¾ red and ___ white make the whole flag.

reteach.say: The whole flag is all four quarters. If three quarters are red, the leftover is exactly one quarter — white. ¾ and ¼ are partners: together they make one whole. What's shaded and what's left always add up to everything!

block.caption: ¾ red + ¼ white = 1 whole flag

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave naming, impostor-spotting and size comparisons.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach, invite the child to fold a REAL strip and overlay the pieces (CPA step down), then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 including one impostor spotted (unequal split rejected) and one size comparison (½ vs ¼ or ⅓ vs ¼) explained with 'more parts means smaller parts' → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'thirds and quarters of shapes'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the pieces weren't checked for EQUAL' or 'the bigger bottom number tricked us'.
Drop a CPA stage: fold a real strip, overlay the pieces.
Give ONE hint: 'Do the parts land exactly on top of each other?'
Re-ask with halves vs quarters only, then build back to thirds.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — let's take a smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Recast shaded shapes as the learner's interests — flag designs, pizza toppings, chocolate flavours, football-shirt stripes. The equal-parts fold test stays in every framing; never change the fractions.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable item (halves vs quarters if needed), then process praise: 'you checked the parts were EQUAL before naming any fraction — that's a real mathematician's habit.' If the real chocolate bar is there, share it fairly in three as the victory lap.

differentiation.support: Fold the same bar into 2 vs 3 to FEEL that thirds are smaller (the KB fix for '⅓ > ½'); use pre-creased strips so the folds land true.
differentiation.stretch: 'Is this split into quarters?' with a deliberately unequal split → no, and say why; show ¾ of a square two DIFFERENT ways.

extension: Make a 'fraction flag' — design a flag that is exactly ¾ one colour and ¼ another; check it with the fold test.
assessmentEvidence: Child folds/shades correct thirds and quarters, identifies ¾, rejects an unequal split, and explains that ½ > ¼ because fewer parts are larger.
revisitLater: Feeds straight into fractions of a QUANTITY next lesson (¼ of 12 shares into 4 piles); quick 'real or impostor?' recall in Lesson 25.
